results.summary: This is a 4-bit ALU implemented in Verilog that performs addition, subtraction, negation, multiplication, and bitwise AND, OR and XOR. Two 4-bit operands are supplied on the eight input pins, and the operation is selected by driving the corresponding bidirectional pin high. The 4-bit result appears on the upper four output pins, while the lower four output pins carry the upper half of the multiplication result. The documentation is brief and does not describe timing, testing or any silicon results.

Spacewar is a scaled-down version of the classic Spacewar game written in Verilog, targeting VGA video output and audio. It reads a SNES-style gamepad over a clocked serial interface and also provides a PWM audio output and XY scope outputs. The pinout matches the Tiny VGA, TT Audio and Gamepad PMOD conventions, so external VGA, audio, SNES controller and scope hardware are required. The documentation is thin: testing is listed as 'Cocotb coming soon' and no silicon results are reported.

This VHDL design translates an SPI stream into eight parallel WS2811 LED strip output channels. A microcontroller drives CS and COPI at roughly 14 MHz, sending interleaved RGB bytes for the eight strips followed by eight null bytes to keep the clock and chip select active. Each of the eight output pins then emits a WS2811 frame for its strip, and the design is flexible about SPI timing. An IceStick was used for testing, and the documentation gives a clear frame format example.

This Verilog design implements a stochastic multiplier, adder and self-multiplier that operate on serial probability-coded bit streams. Binary-weighted two's-complement inputs are converted to stochastic streams, combined, and converted back to a serial binary-weighted output. Two serial input pins feed the computation and four output pins carry the multiply, add, self-multiply and counter-reset signals. Testing requires an ADALM2000 and Python to generate and analyse the serial streams, and the documentation is otherwise sparse.

This Verilog project uses stochastic computing to implement an integrator based on Euler's definition of integration in the unipolar probability domain. Two serial input pins accept stochastic bit streams, and eight output pins expose several sequential, system and test integrator outputs. The suggested test is to hold one input high and the other low and observe the resulting equations on the outputs. An ADALM2000 is listed as the external hardware, and the documentation gives only a brief description of the internal structure.

This Verilog design is a digital stopwatch that counts seconds and minutes and displays them on a multiplexed 4-digit 7-segment display. A clock divider produces a 1 Hz enable from the Tiny Tapeout clock, and start and stop are controlled by two input pins. The segment and decimal-point lines are on the eight output pins, while the four digit-select lines are on the bidirectional pins. It needs a common-anode 7-segment display connected externally, and the documentation describes simulation and hardware testing clearly.

This Verilog design monitors three input signals and asserts an alarm output when all three are active within the same time window of about six seconds at 100 MHz. The three sensor inputs are on the lower input pins and the single response output is on the first output pin. External sensors, buttons or similar sources drive the inputs, and the output can be connected to an LED, display or sounder. The documentation is very short and gives no detail on the timing logic or any test results.

This is a mixed-signal two-class classifier built from analog Gaussian circuits, with both analog and digital inputs. Four digital input pins act as DAC controls, one analog pin supplies a reference voltage, and two analog output pins provide the class currents. Testing involves sweeping the digital DAC inputs and the analog reference while observing the output currents with an oscilloscope or multimeter. The documentation is minimal and does not describe the classifier's accuracy or any measured silicon behaviour.

This SystemVerilog design is a fully combinational adder for 8-bit posit numbers with zero exponent bits. It decodes the two posit operands into fixed-point values and scale factors, aligns and adds them, then re-encodes the rounded result back into posit format. Operand A is supplied on the input pins, operand B on the bidirectional pins, and the sum appears on the output pins. The design was exhaustively verified in simulation against a software reference before fabrication, and post-silicon testing is planned with a microcontroller or DIP switches.

This SystemVerilog design is a fully combinational multiplier for 8-bit posit numbers with zero exponent bits. It decodes the two posit operands into fixed-point values and scale factors, aligns and multiplies them, then re-encodes the rounded product back into posit format. Operand A is supplied on the input pins, operand B on the bidirectional pins, and the product appears on the output pins. The design was exhaustively verified in simulation against a software reference before fabrication, and post-silicon testing is planned with a microcontroller or DIP switches; the description text mistakenly refers to a sum rather than a product.
